title: VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP and INDEX/MATCH
summary: Look up values across sheets with VLOOKUP, XLOOKUP, and INDEX/MATCH, and diagnose the three most common formula error codes.

steps.title: Finding a Driver Name from an Order Row
steps.lede: Your Orders sheet records a driver ID in column F. VLOOKUP and XLOOKUP let you pull the matching driver name from the Drivers sheet automatically.

blocks.text: Suppose your Drivers sheet has driver IDs in its leftmost column and driver names in the column next to it, and your Orders sheet records a driver ID in column F. You want each order row to show the matching driver's name without retyping it. Lookup functions do exactly that: they search one table for a key and return a value from the same row.

VLOOKUP looks up a value in the leftmost column of a range and returns a value from the same row in a column you specify by its position. Its syntax is VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, [range_lookup]). Entering FALSE for range_lookup searches for an exact match; leaving it blank or entering TRUE searches for an approximate match — and TRUE is the default when the argument is omitted. To look up a driver ID exactly, write =VLOOKUP(F2,Drivers!A:B,2,FALSE).

annotations.text: Lookup key column (leftmost) — VLOOKUP searches here

segments.label: Building a VLOOKUP formula: key column, return column, and exact-match argument
segments.summary: A VLOOKUP formula is assembled argument by argument against a sales dataset. The lookup value is a name; the table range covers the salesperson column through the sales column; the column index is set to 3 because the target data sits in the third column of that range. The final argument is explained as the match-type switch: FALSE forces an exact match, which is the right choice in almost all business cases. TRUE, or omitting the argument entirely, triggers approximate matching and should only be used when the data is already sorted — and even then the results may be unreliable. The formula is then made dynamic by pointing the lookup value to a cell so that changing the cell updates the result.

segments.label: Building an XLOOKUP formula: lookup array, return array, and the if_not_found argument
segments.summary: XLOOKUP is introduced as a finding tool: given a name in a cell, it locates that name in a lookup column and returns the corresponding value from a separate return column. The formula is built in argument order — lookup value (pointed to a cell or typed directly), lookup array (the name column, B8:B42), return array (the job-title column, G8:G42) — and returns the correct result immediately. Pointing to a cell rather than hard-coding a value makes the formula reusable. When the lookup value is absent from the data, XLOOKUP returns an #N/A error; the fourth argument, if_not_found, lets you supply a custom message such as 'no such person' instead.

blocks.group_title: Lookup functions in action: VLOOKUP and XLOOKUP

bridge.before: Watch how each argument is chosen and what the match-type argument does in the first clip; in the second, note the separate lookup array and return array — XLOOKUP's key structural difference from VLOOKUP.
bridge.after: Neither clip covers HLOOKUP or XLOOKUP's direction advantage over VLOOKUP; the teaching text fills both gaps. Error values (#N/A) shown in the second clip are a later topic — ignore them here.

steps.title: HLOOKUP and XLOOKUP
steps.lede: HLOOKUP searches across rows instead of down columns. XLOOKUP is a newer alternative that works in any direction and matches exactly by default.

blocks.text: HLOOKUP works like VLOOKUP but searches across the top row of a table and returns a value from a row you specify by its position. Its syntax is HLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, row_index_num, [range_lookup]).

XLOOKUP searches lookup_array for lookup_value and returns the corresponding item from return_array, producing an exact match by default. Its syntax is XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found], [match_mode], [search_mode]). VLOOKUP can only look up a value from left to right, but XLOOKUP works in any direction. The same driver lookup written as =XLOOKUP(F2,Drivers!A:A,Drivers!B:B) already matches exactly, without needing FALSE spelled out.

steps.title: HLOOKUP: Row Index
steps.lede: Test your understanding of HLOOKUP's row_index_num argument.

public.prompt: A summary table has product categories across the top row (row 1) and quarterly totals in rows 2 and 3. You want to retrieve the Q2 total for the 'Logistics' category. Which formula correctly uses HLOOKUP to do this?

opt_b.message: VLOOKUP searches the leftmost column, not the top row. When the lookup values are in the top row, use HLOOKUP instead.

opt_c.message: The row_index_num 2 would return the Q1 row (row 2), not Q2. Q2 is in row 3, so row_index_num should be 3.

opt_d.message: In HLOOKUP the first argument is the lookup_value (the category name), not the row number. The row_index_num is the third argument.

correct.message: Correct! HLOOKUP searches the top row for 'Logistics', then returns the value from row 3 (row_index_num = 3), which is the Q2 row. FALSE forces an exact match.

incorrect.message: HLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, row_index_num, [range_lookup]) searches the top row for the lookup_value and returns the value from the row you specify. Row 1 is the header row, so Q2 data is in row 3.

hints: HLOOKUP is the horizontal counterpart of VLOOKUP: it scans across the top row instead of down the left column.
Count the rows from the top of the table: row 1 = headers, row 2 = Q1, row 3 = Q2.

steps.title: Write VLOOKUP and XLOOKUP Formulas
steps.lede: Use the QuickDeliver Orders and Drivers sheets to write lookup formulas that return driver names.

public.prompt:
The **drivers** sheet has driver IDs in column A and driver names in column B. Cell A1 holds the lookup key **D01**.

**Task 1 — VLOOKUP:** In cell B1, write a VLOOKUP formula that looks up the value in A1 in the drivers sheet (columns A:B) and returns the driver name (column index 2). Use FALSE for an exact match.

**Task 2 — XLOOKUP:** In cell C1, write an XLOOKUP formula that looks up the value in A1 in drivers column A and returns the corresponding value from drivers column B.

tests.message_on_fail: B1 should return 'Amara Okafor' for driver ID D01. Check that your VLOOKUP uses A1 as the lookup value, drivers!A:B as the table, 2 as the column index, and 0 for exact match.
Cell B1 must contain a VLOOKUP formula.
C1 should return 'Amara Okafor' for driver ID D01. Check that your XLOOKUP uses A1 as lookup_value, drivers!A:A as lookup_array, and drivers!B:B as return_array.
Cell C1 must contain an XLOOKUP formula.

correct.message: Well done! Your VLOOKUP correctly uses the key column (A), the table range (drivers!A:B), column index 2, and 0 for exact match. Your XLOOKUP separates the lookup array (drivers!A:A) from the return array (drivers!B:B) and matches exactly by default.

incorrect.message: Check both formulas. VLOOKUP needs: lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, 0 (or FALSE). XLOOKUP needs: lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array. Both should return 'Amara Okafor' for driver ID D01.

hints: For VLOOKUP, the table_array must start with the column containing the lookup key (driver_id in column A of the drivers sheet).
For XLOOKUP, the lookup_array and return_array are separate arguments — you don't need a column index number.

steps.title: When the Key Column Is Not on the Left
steps.lede: VLOOKUP requires the lookup key to be in the leftmost column. When the layout is reversed, INDEX and MATCH work together to handle it.

blocks.text: VLOOKUP only works when the column you're returning a value from sits to the right of the key column. If your Drivers sheet instead had driver names in column A and driver IDs in column B, VLOOKUP couldn't look up an ID and return the name to its left.

MATCH searches for a specified item in a range of cells and returns the relative position of that item within the range. Its syntax is MATCH(lookup_value, lookup_array, [match_type]). Setting match_type to 0 finds an exact match; a match_type of 1, or omitting the argument, finds the largest value less than or equal to lookup_value and requires lookup_array to be sorted in ascending order.
INDEX returns the value of an element in a range or array, selected by its row and column position. The array form's syntax is INDEX(array, row_num, [column_num]).

annotations.text: Return column (driver_name) — sits LEFT of the key
Key column (driver_id) — VLOOKUP cannot look left from here

segments.label: Live demo: INDEX/MATCH formula with an exact-match lookup
segments.summary: A spreadsheet holds employee names in one column and join dates in another; the goal is to return the name for a given date. The presenter builds =INDEX(name column, MATCH(input date, date column, 0)), explaining that MATCH first finds the row position of the date and INDEX then returns the name at that position. The formula is then split into its two parts to show each step: MATCH alone returns 6 (the sixth date), and INDEX alone on the names list returns the sixth name, confirming how the two functions hand off to each other.

blocks.group_title: INDEX and MATCH working together: a two-step lookup

bridge.before: Watch how MATCH produces a row number and INDEX consumes it. The return column (names) sits left of the lookup column (dates) — the exact layout VLOOKUP cannot handle.
bridge.after: The clip shows only exact-match (match_type 0) and does not cover match_type 1 or the sorting requirement; the teaching text covers both.

steps.title: Combining INDEX and MATCH
steps.lede: MATCH finds the row; INDEX retrieves the value. Together they handle any column layout.

blocks.text: VLOOKUP can only look up a value from left to right — the column containing the lookup value must be to the left of the column containing the return value. When the layout isn't built that way, MATCH can find the row position of the key and INDEX can then return the value from any column at that row position. On your Orders sheet, with a driver ID in F2, =INDEX(Drivers!A:A,MATCH(F2,Drivers!B:B,0)) finds the row where that driver ID occurs in column B of the Drivers sheet, then reads the driver name from column A at that same row — something VLOOKUP alone couldn't do on this layout.

steps.title: Write an INDEX/MATCH Formula
steps.lede: Choose the correct INDEX/MATCH formula for a reversed-column layout.

public.prompt: A reference sheet has driver names in column A and driver IDs in column B. You want to look up driver ID 'D04' and return the driver's name. Which formula correctly uses INDEX/MATCH to do this?

opt_b.message: VLOOKUP requires the lookup key to be in the leftmost column of the table. Here the key (driver ID) is in column B, which is to the right of the return value (driver name in column A). VLOOKUP cannot handle this layout.

opt_c.message: This formula looks up 'D04' in column A (driver names) and returns from column B (driver IDs) — the reverse of what you want. The INDEX array should be the column you want to return from (A), and the MATCH lookup_array should be the column containing the key (B).

opt_d.message: match_type 1 finds the largest value less than or equal to the lookup value and requires the array to be sorted ascending — it does not find an exact match. Use 0 for an exact match.

correct.message: Correct! INDEX(A:A, ...) targets the driver name column. MATCH('D04', B:B, 0) finds the exact position of 'D04' in the driver ID column. INDEX then returns the name at that row position.

incorrect.message: INDEX(array, row_num) returns the value at a given row in the array. MATCH(lookup_value, lookup_array, 0) finds the exact position of the key. Set INDEX's array to the column you want to return from (A), and MATCH's lookup_array to the column containing the key (B).

hints: Think of it in two steps: MATCH finds the row number of 'D04' in column B; INDEX uses that row number to fetch the name from column A.
match_type 0 means exact match — always use 0 when looking up a specific ID.

steps.title: Build an INDEX/MATCH Lookup
steps.lede: Given the reversed Drivers layout, write an INDEX/MATCH formula that returns the driver name for a given driver ID.

public.prompt:
The **drivers** sheet has driver names in column A and driver IDs in column B — the key column is to the **right** of the return column, so VLOOKUP cannot be used.

Cell C1 holds the lookup key **D01**.

In cell D1, write an INDEX/MATCH formula that:
- Uses INDEX on column A (the name column) as the array
- Uses MATCH with match_type 0 to find the exact position of C1 in column B
- Returns the driver name that corresponds to driver ID D01

tests.message_on_fail: D1 should return 'Amara Okafor' for driver ID D01. Check that INDEX uses A:A and MATCH uses B:B with match_type 0.
Cell D1 must contain a formula using both INDEX and MATCH.

correct.message: Excellent! INDEX(A:A, MATCH(C1, B:B, 0)) correctly handles the reversed layout: MATCH finds the row of D01 in column B, and INDEX returns the name from column A at that row.

incorrect.message: Remember: INDEX(array, row_num) returns a value from the array at the given row. MATCH(lookup_value, lookup_array, 0) returns the position of the lookup value. Set INDEX's array to A:A (names) and MATCH's lookup_array to B:B (IDs).

hints: Start with the outer function: INDEX(A:A, ...) — this says 'return a value from the driver name column'.
The MATCH inside finds the row: MATCH(C1, B:B, 0) — 'find the exact position of C1 in the driver ID column'.

steps.title: Reading #N/A and #REF! Error Codes
steps.lede: When a formula can't find what it needs or points to a cell that no longer exists, Excel shows an error code instead of a value.

blocks.text: Formulas in your Orders or Drivers sheets sometimes show an error code instead of a value. Each code points at a different kind of problem.

The #N/A error generally indicates that a formula can't find what it's been asked to look for. The most common cause is with XLOOKUP, VLOOKUP, HLOOKUP, LOOKUP, or MATCH functions when the lookup value doesn't exist in the source data. A VLOOKUP for a driver ID that was never entered on the Drivers sheet would show #N/A.

The #REF! error shows when a formula refers to a cell that's not valid, which happens most often when cells that were referenced by formulas get deleted or pasted over. Deleting the amount column that a SUM formula depended on would turn that formula into a #REF! error.

steps.title: The #VALUE! Error and SUM vs. Arithmetic
steps.lede: A text value in a cell can break an arithmetic formula but not a SUM — knowing the difference helps you fix the right thing.

blocks.text: #VALUE! is Excel's way of saying there's something wrong with the way a formula is typed, or something wrong with the cells it's referencing. A formula like =A1+B1+C1 can break and return #VALUE! if any referenced cell contains a non-numeric (text) value, whereas a SUM formula over the same cells ignores the text values and sums only the numeric ones — so typing a stray note into an amount cell breaks a plain + formula but not a SUM over the same range.
If AVERAGE or SUM refer to cells that contain #VALUE! errors, the formulas will result in a #VALUE! error too — so one bad cell's error can spread into a SUM or AVERAGE built on top of it.

steps.title: Seeing Formula Errors Appear and Propagate

segments.label: How #VALUE!, #REF!, and #N/A errors appear in a real spreadsheet
segments.summary: The presenter works through several error codes on a live sheet. For #VALUE!, a subtraction formula breaks the moment a cell holds the text 'missing'; wrapping the same calculation inside SUM makes the error disappear because SUM skips text values. For #REF!, deleting a column that a formula depended on immediately turns that formula into a #REF! error; copying and pasting the formula to a location where its relative reference points off the grid does the same. Two additional errors (#SPILL! and #NAME?) are shown briefly: #SPILL! appears when a spilling function is blocked by a non-empty cell, and #NAME? appears when a function name is mistyped. For #DIV/0!, dividing by an empty cell (treated as zero) triggers the error, and IFERROR is used to suppress it. Finally, #N/A is demonstrated with a VLOOKUP that cannot find 'Limbo' because the correct spelling in the source data is 'Limba'; IFNA is then used to return a custom message instead of the error code.

blocks.group_title: Seeing formula errors appear and propagate on a live sheet

steps.title: Diagnosing #VALUE! Errors
steps.lede: Identify the cause of a #VALUE! error and the fix that avoids it.

public.prompt: Cell D10 contains the formula =D2+D3+D4+D5. The formula returns #VALUE!. You inspect the cells and find that D4 contains the text 'N/A' instead of a number. Which of the following correctly describes the cause and the fix?

options.text: The arithmetic + operator cannot add a text value; replacing the formula with =SUM(D2:D5) would fix it because SUM ignores text values and sums only the numeric ones.
The formula is referencing too many cells; reducing it to =D2+D3 would fix it.
The #VALUE! error means a cell reference is invalid (deleted or moved); re-entering the formula would fix it.
The + operator requires all cells to be formatted as Currency; reformatting D4 as Currency would fix it.

opt_b.message: The number of cells is not the issue. The problem is that D4 contains text. Even =D2+D4 alone would return #VALUE! because of the text in D4.

opt_c.message: A deleted or moved reference causes #REF!, not #VALUE!. #VALUE! indicates a type mismatch — the formula is trying to add a text value.

opt_d.message: Cell formatting does not change the underlying data type. D4 contains the text string 'N/A', not a number, regardless of how it is formatted. SUM would ignore it; the + operator cannot.

correct.message: Correct! The arithmetic + operator cannot handle text, so it returns #VALUE!. SUM(D2:D5) silently skips text values and sums only the numbers — the cleanest fix without removing the text cell.

incorrect.message: #VALUE! means the formula encountered a value of the wrong type. Here, D4 holds text ('N/A') and the + operator cannot add text. Switching to SUM resolves this because SUM ignores non-numeric cells.

hints: Think about what #VALUE! specifically means: something is wrong with the type of a value the formula is using.
SUM and the + operator behave differently when a cell contains text — one ignores it, the other fails.

steps.title: #VALUE! Propagation Through SUM or AVERAGE
steps.lede: Understand how a single error cell can spread into formulas built on top of it.

public.prompt: Cell E5 contains =A5+B5 and returns #VALUE! because B5 holds text. Cell F5 contains =SUM(E5, C5, D5). What does F5 display?

options.text: The sum of C5 and D5 only (SUM skips the error in E5)

opt_b.message: SUM ignores text values in its range, but it does not ignore error values such as #VALUE!. When a cell in SUM's range contains an error, SUM propagates that error.

opt_c.message: SUM does not treat errors as zero. It propagates them. Only text values (like 'N/A') are silently skipped by SUM; error values (like #VALUE!) cause SUM to return the same error.

opt_d.message: #REF! appears when a formula references an invalid cell (e.g., a deleted row). Here the reference is valid; the problem is that E5 itself contains a #VALUE! error, which SUM propagates.

correct.message: Correct! When SUM or AVERAGE reference a cell that already contains a #VALUE! error, they propagate that error rather than skipping it. SUM skips text values but not error values.

incorrect.message: SUM skips plain text values in its range, but it does not skip error values. If any cell in SUM's range contains #VALUE!, SUM returns #VALUE! too. This is error propagation.

hints: There is a difference between a cell containing the text 'N/A' and a cell containing the error #VALUE! — SUM treats them differently.
Think about what happens when SUM encounters an error cell versus a text cell.

steps.title: Diagnose Formula Errors
steps.lede: Given a worksheet with a broken VLOOKUP showing #N/A and a broken addition formula showing #VALUE!, identify the cause of each error.

public.prompt:
This workbook has three broken formulas.

**Fix 1 — #N/A in B8:** The VLOOKUP in B8 returns #N/A because the driver ID in A8 ('D0X') does not exist in the drivers sheet. Change A8 to the correct driver ID **D01** so the VLOOKUP finds a match and returns the driver name.

**Fix 2 — #REF! in C8:** The formula in C8 returns #REF! because it references a cell that is not valid. The formula should sum the values in E1 and F1 (which contain 100 and 200). Replace the #REF! formula in C8 with **=SUM(E1:F1)**.

**Fix 3 — #VALUE! in D9:** The formula =A9+B9+C9 in D9 returns #VALUE! because B9 contains the text 'N/A'. Replace the formula in D9 with one that sums A9:C9 but ignores the text value in B9.

tests.message_on_fail: B8 should return 'Amara Okafor'. Fix A8 to contain the correct driver ID 'D01' so the VLOOKUP finds a match.
C8 should return 300 (100 + 200). Replace the #REF! formula with =SUM(E1:F1).
D9 should return 300 (100 + 200, ignoring the text in B9). Replace the arithmetic formula with a SUM formula.
Cell D9 must use the SUM function to ignore the text value in B9.

correct.message: Well done! You fixed all three errors: correcting the misspelled driver ID resolved the #N/A (the lookup value now exists in the source data), replacing the #REF! formula resolved the invalid cell reference, and switching to SUM resolved the #VALUE! (SUM ignores text values, the + operator does not).

incorrect.message: Check all three fixes. For B8: the VLOOKUP returns #N/A because A8 contains 'D0X' which doesn't exist in the drivers sheet — change A8 to 'D01'. For C8: replace the #REF! formula with =E1+F1 to sum the values in E1 and F1. For D9: replace the + formula with =SUM(A9:C9) to ignore the text in B9.

hints: For the #N/A error: compare the value in A8 character by character with the driver IDs in the drivers sheet.
For the #REF! error: use SUM to add E1 (100) and F1 (200) to get 300.
For the #VALUE! error: SUM and the + operator behave differently when a cell contains text — SUM skips it, + fails.

steps.title: Lookups and Error Codes — Key Points
steps.lede: You can now look up values across sheets and read the three most common formula error codes.

blocks.text: VLOOKUP searches the leftmost column and returns a value by column position; use FALSE for an exact match. XLOOKUP works in any direction and matches exactly by default. When the return column sits left of the key column, combine INDEX and MATCH: MATCH finds the row position, INDEX retrieves the value. #N/A means the lookup value was not found; #REF! means a referenced cell is invalid; #VALUE! means a wrong data type — and, as covered earlier, SUM or AVERAGE over cells containing #VALUE! errors also return #VALUE!.

remediation_steps.title: VLOOKUP vs. HLOOKUP: Columns vs. Rows
remediation_steps.lede: A clear contrast between the two functions shows which argument controls the return position.

blocks.text: VLOOKUP searches down the leftmost column and uses col_index_num to pick which column to return — =VLOOKUP(F2,Drivers!A:B,2,FALSE) returns the value in the 2nd column. HLOOKUP searches across the top row and uses row_index_num to pick which row to return — =HLOOKUP("Delivered",A1:D3,2,FALSE) returns the value in the 2nd row. The key difference: VLOOKUP counts columns; HLOOKUP counts rows.

remediation_steps.title: INDEX and MATCH: Two Steps, One Result
remediation_steps.lede: See how MATCH produces a row number and INDEX uses it to return a value.

blocks.text: On the QuickDeliver Orders sheet, driver ID D03 is in cell F5. MATCH(F5,Drivers!B:B,0) searches column B of the Drivers sheet for D03 and returns its row position — say 4. INDEX(Drivers!A:A,4) then returns the value in row 4 of column A, which is the driver name. The full formula =INDEX(Drivers!A:A,MATCH(F5,Drivers!B:B,0)) combines both steps. VLOOKUP cannot do this because the return column (A) is to the left of the key column (B).

remediation_steps.title: #VALUE!: Text in a Number Cell
remediation_steps.lede: See the exact difference between an arithmetic formula and SUM when one cell holds text.

blocks.text: Suppose the QuickDeliver Orders sheet had an amount cell that held the text "N/A" instead of a number. A formula like =D2+D16 would return #VALUE! because the + operator cannot add text. But a formula like =SUM(D2:D21) would return a total because SUM ignores text values and sums only the numeric ones. Switching from + to SUM resolves the #VALUE! error without removing the text cell.

remediation_steps.title: #VALUE! Spreads Upward
remediation_steps.lede: One bad cell's error can propagate into any formula that references it.

blocks.text: If cell D16 already contains a #VALUE! error, then =AVERAGE(D2:D21) will also return #VALUE! — not a number — because AVERAGE and SUM propagate errors from cells they reference. The error in D16 spreads into any formula built on top of it. Fixing D16 (for example, by replacing the text with a valid number) clears the error from all dependent formulas at once.
